name: The Great Lakes
subtitle: One fifth of the world's fresh surface water

mnemonic.note: Five letters, five lakes. HOMES gets you the names; going west to east gets you the order they drain: Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, Ontario.

items.label: Ontario
items.note: Smallest, and the last one before the Atlantic

items.label: Michigan
items.note: The only one entirely inside the US

items.label: Superior
items.note: Largest freshwater lake on Earth by area

story: The Great Lakes are what a mile-thick ice sheet leaves behind. Glaciers gouged out five basins, then melted into them. Everything drains one way, downhill from Superior to Ontario and out the St. Lawrence to the Atlantic - except for the 325-foot drop between Erie and Ontario, which is Niagara Falls.
nameStory: The lakes carry a jumble of languages: Superior is French for 'upper,' Michigan and Huron come from Native words for large water and for the Wendat people, Erie from the Erie nation, and Ontario from an Iroquoian word for 'beautiful lake.' Four hundred years of naming, all still visible on one map.
keyFacts: Together they hold about 21% of the world's fresh surface water.
Only Lake Michigan lies entirely within the United States; the other four are shared with Canada.
Lake Superior alone could cover all of North and South America in a foot of water.
They are young: the last ice sheet only finished melting out of these basins about 10,000 years ago.
The Great Lakes coastline is longer than the US Atlantic and Pacific coasts combined.
whyItMatters: Roughly 40 million people drink from these lakes. Because a border runs down the middle of four of them, protecting that water requires two countries to agree, which they formalized in the Great Lakes Compact.

name: The Rocky Mountains
subtitle: The spine of the continent
story: The Rockies run about 3,000 miles from New Mexico into Canada, and they do something no other American range does: they decide where water goes. Rain falling on one side of the crest ends up in the Pacific. Rain falling a few feet away on the other side ends up in the Atlantic or the Gulf of Mexico. That crest is the Continental Divide, and standing on it means standing between two oceans.
nameStory: The name is a translation. French traders called the people living in them 'les Montagnes Rocheuses,' probably rendering a Cree term. English speakers shortened it to the Rockies and it stuck.
keyFacts: The Rockies are young mountains - roughly 55 to 80 million years old, compared to the Appalachians' 480 million.
Colorado's Mount Elbert, 14,440 feet, is the highest point in the whole range.
The Divide is not always a knife edge; in Wyoming's Great Divide Basin it splits and surrounds land that drains to neither ocean.
Snowpack in the Rockies is the water supply for most of the American West.
whyItMatters: Almost every major western river - the Colorado, the Rio Grande, the Missouri, the Columbia's tributaries - starts as snow in these mountains. A warm winter here becomes a water crisis a thousand miles downstream.

name: The Continental Divide
subtitle: The line where water chooses an ocean
story: Pour a glass of water on the Divide and it has to pick a side. West means the Pacific. East means the Gulf of Mexico or the Atlantic. There is no third option and no going back. The Divide runs the length of the Americas, and in the US it threads down the crest of the Rockies from Glacier National Park to the Mexican border.
nameStory: Older maps call it the 'Great Divide,' and trappers called it simply 'the backbone of the world.' The idea it describes - a hydrologic divide - is why the Louisiana Purchase was defined the way it was: Jefferson bought a watershed, everything that drained into the Mississippi, and the Divide was its western wall.
keyFacts: Triple Divide Peak in Montana sends water to the Pacific, the Atlantic, and the Arctic - the only such point in the United States.
The Continental Divide Trail follows it for about 3,100 miles from Mexico to Canada.
In Wyoming's Great Divide Basin the Divide splits in two and rejoins, enclosing land whose water reaches no ocean at all.
Chicago sits just barely on the Atlantic side of a much smaller divide - which is why a canal could connect the Great Lakes to the Mississippi.

name: The Appalachian Mountains
subtitle: The oldest mountains in America
story: The Appalachians are old almost beyond imagining - around 480 million years old, formed when the landmass that would become Africa slammed into North America. They were once as tall and sharp as the Himalayas. Everything you see now is the worn-down stump. Here is the part that sticks: when the Atlantic Ocean opened and tore the continents apart, it tore the range in half. The other half of the Appalachians is in Scotland, Ireland, and Norway. The Scottish Highlands are the same mountains.
nameStory: The name came from the wrong end of the continent. Spanish explorers in northern Florida heard of a people called the Apalachee, wrote the name on their maps, and it drifted northward until it labeled a range stretching 1,500 miles into Canada.
keyFacts: About 480 million years old - roughly seven times older than the Rockies.
The same range continues in Scotland, Ireland, Norway, and Morocco; the Atlantic split it apart.
Mount Mitchell in North Carolina, 6,684 feet, is the highest point east of the Mississippi.
The range is not one ridge but dozens of parallel ridges, which is why crossing it was so difficult.
The Great Smokies are the most visited national park in the United States.
whyItMatters: For 150 years these mountains were a wall that held British colonies against the coast. Britain's Proclamation of 1763 forbade settlement past the crest, and colonial anger about that line was one of the grievances that led to revolution. Where the range could be crossed - the Cumberland Gap, the Mohawk Valley - is where the roads, canals, railroads, and cities went.

name: The Appalachian Trail
subtitle: Georgia to Maine on foot
story: About 2,197 miles of footpath from Springer Mountain in Georgia to Mount Katahdin in Maine, through fourteen states. A forester named Benton MacKaye proposed it in 1921 as an escape valve for people trapped in industrial cities. Walking the whole thing takes five to seven months, and roughly one in four people who start actually finish.
nameStory: It takes its name from the mountains it follows, which took theirs from a Florida people the mountains never touched. The length changes slightly every year as sections are rerouted, so the trail has no permanent official distance.
keyFacts: Fourteen states: Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, New York, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine.
Virginia holds about a quarter of the entire trail - more than any other state.
Total elevation gain over the full hike is roughly equivalent to climbing Everest sixteen times from sea level.
Harpers Ferry, West Virginia is trail headquarters and the traditional psychological halfway point, though not the true midpoint.
It is maintained almost entirely by volunteers - tens of thousands of hours a year.

name: The Sierra Nevada
subtitle: One enormous tilted slab of granite
story: The Sierra Nevada is not a folded range like the Appalachians. It is a single block of granite about 400 miles long that was pushed up along a fault on its eastern edge and tipped westward, like a trapdoor. That is why the western slope is a long gentle climb and the eastern face drops off in a wall - and why the gold was where it was. Streams cutting down that long west slope concentrated flecks of gold into the foothill gravel, which is exactly where James Marshall found some in a millrace in 1848.
nameStory: Spanish for 'snowy saw-toothed range.' Sailors and explorers named it from far away, based on the jagged white skyline they could see from the Central Valley without ever going near it.
keyFacts: Mount Whitney, 14,505 feet, is the highest point in the contiguous United States.
The range's rain shadow is why Nevada, immediately downwind, is the driest state in the country.
Giant sequoias - the largest trees on Earth by volume - grow naturally only on the Sierra's western slope.
Sierra snowpack supplies roughly 30% of California's water, stored as snow and released slowly all summer.
The Donner Party was trapped by Sierra snow in the winter of 1846-47 at what is now Donner Pass.
whyItMatters: The gold found in these foothills in 1848 brought about 300,000 people to California in a few years. It was so overwhelming that California skipped the territorial stage entirely and became a state in 1850 - which forced the Compromise of 1850 and pushed the country another step toward civil war.

name: Denali / Mount McKinley
subtitle: The highest peak in North America - and a live naming dispute
story: At 20,310 feet it is the highest mountain in North America, and by one measure the most dramatic on Earth: it rises about 18,000 feet from the lowlands at its base, a taller vertical wall than Everest presents from the Tibetan plateau. It also has two names, and which one you use is a live political question rather than a settled fact.
nameStory: The Koyukon Athabascan people, who have lived in its shadow for centuries, call it Denali - 'the high one.' In 1896 a gold prospector named it Mount McKinley after William McKinley, then a presidential candidate, who had never been to Alaska. That name was made official in 1917 and stood for decades while Alaska pushed to change it back.

namingTimeline.label: Denali
namingTimeline.detail: Koyukon Athabascan name meaning 'the high one,' in use long before any European saw the mountain.

namingTimeline.label: Mount McKinley
namingTimeline.detail: A prospector names it for presidential candidate William McKinley, who never visited Alaska.

namingTimeline.label: Mount McKinley
namingTimeline.detail: Federally recognized when Mount McKinley National Park is established.

namingTimeline.label: Denali
namingTimeline.detail: Alaska officially adopts Denali and formally asks the federal government to do the same.

namingTimeline.label: Split names
namingTimeline.detail: The park is renamed Denali National Park and Preserve, but the mountain stays McKinley federally.

namingTimeline.label: Denali
namingTimeline.detail: The Obama administration renames the mountain Denali.

namingTimeline.label: Mount McKinley
namingTimeline.detail: An executive order under the Trump administration renames it Mount McKinley in January.

keyFacts: 20,310 feet - the highest point in North America.
Measured from its own base rather than from sea level, its rise is greater than Everest's.
The national park is named Denali National Park and Preserve, and that has not changed regardless of what the mountain is called.
Alaska's state government and many Alaska Natives have used and continue to use Denali.
The federal name as of this deck's last update is Mount McKinley.
whyItMatters: This is a real, unresolved dispute, and it is worth understanding rather than picking a side on. One argument is that the original Koyukon name has priority and that the mountain was renamed for a politician with no connection to it. The other is that the McKinley name carries over a century of federal usage and honors an assassinated president. Both names are in wide use, and the federal name has now changed three times in fifty years. Geography is not only landforms - it is also who gets to name them.

name: The Mississippi River
subtitle: Minnesota to the Gulf, and the line America divides itself on
story: It starts in northern Minnesota at Lake Itasca as a stream about three feet wide that you can wade across in ten steps, and ends 2,340 miles later spilling into the Gulf of Mexico through a delta of mud. Between those two points it drains 41% of the continental United States - water from 31 states and two Canadian provinces, everything between the Rockies and the Appalachians, funnels into this one channel.
nameStory: From the Ojibwe 'misi-ziibi,' the great river - a name given near its source, over a thousand miles from where most Americans ever encounter it.
keyFacts: 2,340 miles long; a drop of water takes about 90 days to travel the whole thing.
Its basin covers 31 states and 2 Canadian provinces - about 1.2 million square miles.
It was the western border of the United States from 1783 until the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.
Taking Vicksburg in 1863 gave the Union control of the entire river and cut the Confederacy in two.
At Lake Itasca it is ankle deep; at New Orleans it is nearly 200 feet deep.
whyItMatters: The Mississippi is actively trying to abandon its channel and switch into the Atchafalaya, a shorter and steeper route to the Gulf. If it succeeded, New Orleans and Baton Rouge would be left on a saltwater inlet with no river. One Army Corps of Engineers installation, the Old River Control Structure, is what prevents it. The economy of an entire region rests on a piece of concrete holding a river in a channel it does not want to be in.

name: The Grand Canyon
subtitle: A mile deep, and nearly two billion years old at the bottom
story: The canyon is 277 river miles long, up to 18 miles wide, and about a mile deep. The trick to understanding it is that the canyon is young and the rock is ancient. The Colorado River has only been cutting here for five or six million years. But the rock exposed at the very bottom, the Vishnu Schist, is around 1.8 billion years old - close to half the age of the Earth. Hiking down to the river is walking backward through nearly two billion years.
nameStory: Spanish scouts reached the rim in 1540, called it a 'gran canon,' failed to find any way down, and left. The English name was fixed by John Wesley Powell, who ran the entire river through it in wooden boats in 1869 - having lost an arm at Shiloh seven years before.
keyFacts: The rims are about 10 miles apart, but driving between them is 215 miles and takes five hours.
The North Rim is roughly 1,000 feet higher than the South Rim and is closed by snow much of the year.
The Havasupai have lived in and around the canyon for more than 800 years and still do.
It is not the deepest canyon in the country - Hells Canyon in Idaho is deeper - but it is the widest and most completely exposed.
About 40 major rock layers are visible from rim to river.
whyItMatters: Glen Canyon Dam, just upstream, changed the river that made the canyon. The Colorado used to run warm, red, and full of silt, and it flooded every spring. Now it runs cold and clear year-round because water is drawn from deep in the reservoir behind the dam. Native fish have largely vanished and the beaches are washing away, so managers periodically release artificial floods to try to rebuild them.

name: The Colorado River
subtitle: The most fought-over river in America
story: It runs 1,450 miles from the Colorado Rockies toward the Gulf of California - except it usually never gets there. So much water is pulled out for cities and farms that the river dries up in the Mexican desert, often about 100 miles short of the sea. The river that carved the Grand Canyon can no longer reach the ocean.
nameStory: Spanish for 'colored red,' after the silt it carried. Glen Canyon Dam now traps that silt, so the river below it runs cold and clear. The name describes a river that no longer exists.
keyFacts: About 40 million people across seven states and Mexico drink from it.
The 1922 Colorado River Compact split the water during an unusually wet decade, so it promised out more water than the river actually carries. Every drop is legally spoken for, and then some.
Lake Mead and Lake Powell are the two largest reservoirs in the United States, and both have dropped far below capacity.
Its delta in Mexico, once a huge wetland, is now mostly dry salt flat.
whyItMatters: Seven states, thirty tribal nations and Mexico all hold rights to this one river, allocated under a hundred-year-old deal based on water that was never there. Renegotiating it is one of the hardest political problems in the American West.

name: Chesapeake Bay
subtitle: A drowned river valley, and the largest estuary in America
story: The Chesapeake is not really a bay in the ordinary sense. It is the Susquehanna River's old valley, flooded when the ice age ended and sea level rose some 400 feet. The shape you see on a map is a river channel underwater - trace the bay and you are tracing a river that stopped existing at that level 10,000 years ago.
nameStory: From an Algonquian word usually given as 'great shellfish bay.' Oysters were once so abundant that their reefs were a hazard to shipping, and colonists described having to steer around them.
keyFacts: 200 miles long, and in places only about 30 feet deep.
Its watershed covers parts of six states plus DC - some 64,000 square miles, draining about 150 rivers and streams.
An asteroid struck near the mouth of the bay about 35 million years ago, and the crater still influences where the channel sits.
The oyster population is a small fraction of what it was in 1900, and oysters filter the water, so losing them made the water murkier.
whyItMatters: Fertiliser and manure washing off farms hundreds of miles inland feed algae blooms that strip oxygen from the bay, creating summer dead zones. Fixing it needs six states that share nothing else to agree, which is why the Chesapeake Bay Program is studied as a model for governing a whole watershed.

name: The Mojave & Sonoran Deserts
subtitle: Two deserts side by side, and the hottest air ever recorded
story: The Southwest has two very different deserts touching each other, and you can tell them apart by looking at the plants. The Mojave is higher, cold in winter, and belongs to the Joshua tree. The Sonoran is lower, hotter, gets two rainy seasons instead of one, and is the only place on Earth where the saguaro cactus grows wild. Cross the line between them and the vegetation changes completely.
nameStory: Mojave comes from the Pipa Aha Macav, 'the people who live along the water' - a name about a river, attached to a desert. Sonoran is named for the Mexican state next door. Both deserts exist for the same reason: mountains to the west wring the rain out of Pacific storms before they arrive.
keyFacts: Death Valley recorded 134 degrees Fahrenheit in 1913 - the highest air temperature ever measured anywhere on Earth.
Joshua trees grow only in the Mojave. Saguaros grow only in the Sonoran. Neither crosses into the other's desert.
The Sonoran gets both winter rain and a summer monsoon, which makes it the greenest desert in North America.
A saguaro can take 60 years to grow its first arm and can live over 150 years.
whyItMatters: Phoenix and Las Vegas are among the fastest-growing metros in the country and both sit in these deserts, running on Colorado River water and air conditioning. They are a bet that engineering can keep outrunning the climate.

name: The Great Plains
subtitle: Where the rain stops
story: Draw a line straight down the 100th meridian, through the middle of the Dakotas, Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. East of that line you get roughly enough rain to farm the ordinary way. West of it you do not. That invisible boundary is arguably the most important line in American agriculture - and as the climate warms it has been creeping east.
nameStory: Stephen Long's 1820 expedition labelled the region the 'Great American Desert' on its map, and that one phrase kept settlers away for decades. It was never a desert. It was grassland, whose deep roots were the only thing holding thin dry soil in place.
keyFacts: The 100th meridian roughly marks 20 inches of rain a year, the practical limit for farming without irrigation.
Plowing up the grass removed the roots holding the soil down. When drought hit in the 1930s the topsoil simply blew away, and the Dust Bowl was the result.
The Ogallala Aquifer under the plains is being pumped far faster than rain refills it; in places it has already been drained past the point of use.
Less than 4% of the original tallgrass prairie survives anywhere.
whyItMatters: The Dust Bowl was a man-made disaster - the result of farming a grassland as though it were Ohio. It produced the Soil Conservation Service and the idea that how you treat land is a public matter, not only a private one.

name: The Everglades
subtitle: A river 60 miles wide and six inches deep
story: The Everglades looks like a swamp and is not one. It is a river. Water leaves Lake Okeechobee and moves south across a limestone shelf so nearly level that it falls about two inches per mile. The whole sheet of water is flowing - just far too slowly to see. Marjory Stoneman Douglas gave it the name that finally made people understand it in 1947: the River of Grass.
nameStory: A 'glade' is an old English word for an open grassy clearing in a forest. Early surveyors wrote 'River Glades' and then 'Ever Glades' on their maps - glades that went on forever, because nobody could find the far side.
keyFacts: Water takes months to travel from Lake Okeechobee to Florida Bay.
Sawgrass is not grass at all - it is a sedge, and its edges really will cut you.
It is the only place on Earth where alligators and crocodiles live in the same water.
Roughly half the historic Everglades has been drained for farmland and cities.
whyItMatters: For a century the Everglades was treated as wasted land to be drained. Reversing that is now the largest ecosystem restoration ever attempted anywhere, and it has to work while South Florida's drinking water and its defence against storm surge both depend on it.

name: Tornado Alley
subtitle: Where three air masses collide with nothing in the way
story: The central United States gets more tornadoes than the rest of the world combined, and the reason is an accident of terrain. Warm wet air pushes north off the Gulf of Mexico. Cold dry air drops south out of Canada. Hot dry air comes east off the Rockies and rides over the top of both. Nowhere else on Earth stacks those three so reliably - because nowhere else has a thousand miles of flat ground with no east-west mountain range to keep them apart.
nameStory: Not an official region and not on any government map. The phrase came out of a 1952 US Air Force research project on forecasting tornado risk, and meteorologists have argued ever since about where it is - and whether it is moving.
keyFacts: The US averages around 1,200 tornadoes a year, more than every other country combined.
Europe and Asia have east-west mountain ranges that block this collision. North America's ranges run north-south, which lets the air masses drive straight at each other.
Peak season moves north through spring - Texas in March, the Dakotas by June.
'Dixie Alley' in the Southeast gets fewer tornadoes but deadlier ones, because more of them come at night and are hidden by trees and rain.
whyItMatters: Tornado activity has been shifting east out of the classic Plains alley and into the Southeast, where there are more people, more trees blocking the view, and more housing that cannot survive a strong storm.

name: The Rio Grande Border
subtitle: What happens when your border is a river that moves
story: For about 1,250 of the 1,954 miles of the US-Mexico border, the boundary is a river. That is a problem, because rivers wander. When the Rio Grande shifted its channel in the 1860s, roughly 600 acres of Mexico ended up on the American side at El Paso, and Mexico spent the next century demanding it back. The Chamizal dispute was not settled until 1963, and the fix was to pour the river into a concrete channel so it could never move again.
nameStory: It is the Rio Grande in the United States and the Rio Bravo del Norte in Mexico - 'the great river' on one bank, 'the fierce river' on the other. One river with two names, depending on which side you are standing on.
keyFacts: About 1,900 miles long overall; roughly 1,250 of those miles are an international boundary.
It became the border under the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo that ended the Mexican-American War.
In dry years, irrigation takes so much water that stretches of the 'border' are a sandy trench you can walk across.
A 1970 treaty finally fixed the boundary in place no matter how the channel moves in future.
whyItMatters: Nearly every argument about the southern border is really an argument about this river - where it runs, who may cross it, and what a boundary means when the thing marking it is water that shifts, floods and sometimes disappears.

name: The 49th Parallel
subtitle: The longest straight line between two countries
story: Most of the US-Canada border is not a river or a ridge. It is a line of latitude - 49 degrees north - running about 1,260 miles from Minnesota to the Pacific. It was agreed by negotiators in a room in 1818 and simply drawn. Which is why it produces absurdities: Point Roberts, Washington, sits just below the line on the tip of a Canadian peninsula, so the only way to drive there from the rest of America is to leave the country and come back.
nameStory: Named only for its latitude. The 1844 campaign slogan 'Fifty-four forty or fight!' demanded the border be pushed far north to 54 degrees 40 minutes. The 1846 Oregon Treaty settled on 49 instead, and nobody fought.
keyFacts: The full US-Canada border is 5,525 miles, the longest between any two countries on Earth.
Minnesota's Northwest Angle is the only part of the lower 48 north of the 49th parallel - the result of a treaty written using a map that put the source of the Mississippi in the wrong place.
A 20-foot strip is kept permanently cleared of trees along the border so the line stays visible from the ground.
It is often described as the world's longest undefended border.
whyItMatters: It is the clearest example anywhere of a border drawn by mathematics rather than geography. It splits watersheds, towns and one library down the middle, and it works anyway - which is itself worth noticing.

name: The Mason-Dixon Line
subtitle: A property dispute that became the North-South divide
story: Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon were English astronomers hired to settle a dull argument: the Penn and Calvert families could not agree where Pennsylvania ended and Maryland began. From 1763 to 1767 the two men surveyed a line by the stars and planted milestones shipped from England. Eighty years later that arbitrary property boundary had become the border between free states and slave states, and 'below the Mason-Dixon' still means the South.
nameStory: Just the two surveyors' surnames. They also laid out the Twelve-Mile Circle around New Castle, Delaware - the only circular state boundary in America. Whether 'Dixie' comes from Dixon is argued about and has never been settled.
keyFacts: 233 miles, surveyed over four years using stars rather than landmarks.
Some of the original limestone milestones are still standing in fields and hedgerows.
The line sits at latitude 39 degrees 43 minutes - not a round number, because it was fixed by the Delaware circle, not chosen.
Mason and Dixon had to stop when their Native guides refused to go further west into contested territory.
whyItMatters: Two astronomers settling a real estate quarrel accidentally drew the line the country would split along. It is the cleanest demonstration that borders acquire meanings nobody intended when they were made.

name: Four Corners
subtitle: The only place in America where four states touch
story: Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah all meet at a single point - the only quadripoint in the United States. It exists because by the time the Southwest was being organised, surveyors had instruments good enough to just draw rectangles, so Congress did. Older states follow rivers and mountain crests; these four follow lines of latitude and longitude, and rectangles have corners.
nameStory: Purely descriptive, and the description hides a good argument. The monument sits about 1,800 feet from where modern GPS says the corner mathematically belongs. It does not matter: the Supreme Court has held that the markers the original 1875 surveyors planted define the boundary. The corner is legally wherever they said it was.
keyFacts: The only point in the country where you can stand in four states at once.
It sits on land held by the Navajo Nation and the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, who run the monument.
Colorado and Wyoming are the only two states whose borders are entirely straight lines - and Colorado's southwest corner is this one.
The 'error' gets rediscovered by the public every few years and is reported as a scandal each time.
whyItMatters: Four Corners is a useful reminder that a border is a legal fact rather than a physical one. The line is where a surveyor's chain stopped in 1875, and being able to prove that is wrong changes nothing.

name: The BosWash Megalopolis
subtitle: Six hundred miles of almost continuous city
story: From Boston to Washington runs a nearly unbroken band of urban development: Boston, Providence, Hartford, New York, Newark, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Washington. Around 50 million people - close to one American in six - on under 2% of the country's land. There is a reason they line up so neatly. They all sit on the Fall Line, the place where rivers tumble off the hard rock of the Piedmont onto the coastal plain. That was the furthest a ship could sail upriver, and the first place you could put a water wheel. Every one of those cities is a port that could also run a mill.
nameStory: Geographer Jean Gottmann borrowed 'Megalopolis' in 1961 - Greek for 'great city,' and also the name of a real ancient town in Arcadia that tried to unite its region and failed. 'BosWash' was coined a few years later by a futurist compressing Boston and Washington into one word.
keyFacts: Roughly 50 million people, about one in six Americans.
The Fall Line explains the placement of nearly every city in the chain - it is where boats had to stop and where mills could be built.
The Northeast Corridor rail line strings the whole thing together and is the busiest passenger railway in the country.
It holds the nation's political capital and its financial capital, about 100 miles apart.
whyItMatters: Gottmann's argument was that this was a genuinely new kind of settlement - not one city, but no longer separate cities either. Most of the world's population now lives in something shaped like it.

name: The Sun Belt Shift
subtitle: Air conditioning moved the country
story: In 1950 the Northeast and Midwest held most of America's people and most of its political power. Since then the population has swung hard south and west - Texas, Florida, Arizona, Georgia, the Carolinas, Nevada. The biggest single reason is unglamorous. Affordable air conditioning made hot places liveable in August, and once they were liveable, cheap land and cheap energy did the rest. Phoenix had about 107,000 people in 1950. It has well over 1.6 million now.
nameStory: The political analyst Kevin Phillips popularised 'Sun Belt' in 1969, and he was describing a voting bloc at least as much as a climate zone. The name arrived because the shift was already changing elections.
keyFacts: Every census since 1950 has moved House seats - and therefore electoral votes - from the Northeast and Midwest to the South and West.
Texas and Florida gained seats after the 2020 census; New York and California lost them.
The shift depends on water and electricity supplies that are now under real strain in exactly the places growing fastest.
Interstate highways and, later, cheap air travel made distance from the old industrial core matter much less.
whyItMatters: This is geography rewriting political power on a ten-year clock. Where people choose to live decides how many votes each state gets in Congress and in presidential elections, so a technology as ordinary as air conditioning ends up reshaping who governs.

name: Chicago, the Rail Hub
subtitle: Why the country's railroads all bend toward one city
story: Look at a map of American freight rail and everything converges on Chicago. That is geography, not business luck. Lake Michigan is 300 miles of water pointing straight down into the middle of the country, so any east-west route has to go around it, and going around the southern tip is far shorter. Then, just southwest of the city, there is a low swampy divide where the Great Lakes watershed almost touches the Mississippi's - close enough that in a wet year you could float a canoe between two oceans' worth of drainage. One spot became the hinge between eastern shipping and the entire western interior.
nameStory: From the Miami-Illinois word 'shikaakwa,' a wild onion that grew thick in those marshes. The third-largest city in America is named after a smelly plant nobody wanted to walk through.
keyFacts: Chicago is still the busiest rail hub in North America; a huge share of US freight passes through it.
The Illinois and Michigan Canal opened in 1848 across that low divide, finally connecting the Great Lakes to the Mississippi.
The railroads invented standard time zones in 1883 because they could not write timetables otherwise. The meeting that did it was held in Chicago.
Freight trains can still take longer to cross Chicago than to reach it from the east coast.
whyItMatters: Time zones were created by a private industry to solve a scheduling problem, and most of the country simply went along with it. Congress did not make them law until 1918 - 35 years after everyone was already using them.

name: Los Angeles and Its Water
subtitle: A city that outgrew its river, then took someone else's
story: Los Angeles sits in a semi-arid basin with one modest river and about 15 inches of rain a year. By 1900 it had already outgrown that. So the city quietly bought up land and water rights in the Owens Valley, 230 miles north in the shadow of the Sierra Nevada, and built an aqueduct to bring the water down using nothing but gravity. Owens Valley farms dried up. Owens Lake turned into a dust flat. Los Angeles became the second-largest city in the country. Almost every drop it drinks comes from somewhere else.
nameStory: Founded in 1781 as El Pueblo de Nuestra Senora la Reina de los Angeles - the town of Our Lady the Queen of the Angels - on the banks of a river the Spanish called the Porciuncula. That river is still there, running through the city inside a concrete channel.
keyFacts: The Los Angeles Aqueduct opened in 1913: 233 miles, entirely gravity-fed, no pumps.
Owens Lake became the largest single source of dust pollution in the United States, and LA now spends heavily keeping it damp.
The city also draws from the Colorado River and from Northern California - three separate long-distance supplies.
After deadly floods in 1938 the Los Angeles River was lined with concrete, which is why it looks like a drainage ditch in films.
whyItMatters: This became the template for water in the American West: a growing city buys the water rights of a rural valley that cannot outvote it, and moves the water hundreds of miles. Nearly every western water fight since has followed the same shape.

name: The Erie Canal
subtitle: The ditch that made New York City
story: In 1825 New York finished a 363-mile canal from Albany on the Hudson to Buffalo on Lake Erie. It worked because of a geographic fluke: the Mohawk Valley is the only near-sea-level gap through the entire Appalachian chain, which runs 1,500 miles without another one. Suddenly midwestern grain could reach the Atlantic without ever climbing a mountain. Freight costs collapsed by about 95%, New York overtook every rival port, and the interior of the continent was open.
nameStory: Named for the lake at its western end, which is named for the Erie nation. Opponents called it 'Clinton's Ditch' after Governor DeWitt Clinton, who staked his career on it. The nickname stopped being an insult about a year after it opened.
keyFacts: 363 miles and 83 locks, dug largely by hand by men with shovels and mules.
Moving a ton of freight from Buffalo to New York City fell from around $100 to about $10, and from three weeks to one.
It paid back its entire construction cost in under a decade.
It is why upstate New York is full of classical names - Syracuse, Rome, Utica, Ithaca - laid out by surveyors during a fashion for antiquity.
whyItMatters: Before the canal, Philadelphia, Baltimore and New Orleans were all serious rivals to New York. Afterwards there was no contest. A single engineering project decided which American city would become the largest, and it has stayed decided for 200 years.

name: Route 66
subtitle: Chicago to Santa Monica, and the road out of the Dust Bowl
story: Route 66 ran 2,448 miles from Chicago to the Pacific at Santa Monica, across eight states. It mattered most in the 1930s, when Dust Bowl families loaded everything they owned onto a truck and drove west on it looking for work in California. Steinbeck called it the mother road, the road of flight. Then the Interstates were built to bypass the towns instead of running through them, and in 1985 Route 66 was decommissioned - taken off the map entirely. It survives as nostalgia and a very well-signposted ghost.
nameStory: The number was very nearly 60. Planners argued over it for months, and 66 won partly because it was still unassigned and partly because it simply sounded better. America's most famous road is named after a number chosen to end a bureaucratic argument.
keyFacts: 2,448 miles across eight states - though Kansas got only about 13 of them.
It was one of the first US highways paved end to end, finished in 1938.
Officially removed from the highway system in 1985, after the Interstates made it redundant.
The towns that boomed because the road went through them mostly emptied out when the Interstate went around them.
whyItMatters: Route 66 is the clearest case of infrastructure deciding which places live and which die. The same country that made those towns by routing a road through them unmade them by routing the next road elsewhere.

name: The Transcontinental Railroad
subtitle: Six days instead of six months
story: Before 1869, crossing the continent meant four to six months in a wagon, or a sea voyage all the way around South America. On May 10, 1869, the Central Pacific building east and the Union Pacific building west met at Promontory Summit in Utah, and the journey became about six days. Nothing else in American history compressed distance that fast. The hard part was the Sierra Nevada: solid granite, tunnelled through by hand and black powder, in winters that buried the work camps.
nameStory: Officially just the Pacific Railroad. The golden spike driven at the meeting was ceremonial - it was pulled straight back out and the rails were joined with ordinary iron, because gold is far too soft to hold a railroad together.
keyFacts: About 1,900 miles of track laid in six years.

Chinese labourers made up the large majority of the Central Pacific's workforce and did the most dangerous work in the Sierra. Many died, and they were left out of the official story and the famous photograph for over a century.
The railroad companies were paid by the mile, which is one reason some of the route wanders.
Standard time zones followed in 1883, because a national railway is impossible without them.
whyItMatters: The railroad made the West governable and settlement unstoppable, and it did so at enormous cost to the Plains nations. It carried hunters who destroyed the bison herds within about fifteen years, and without the bison the economies and independence of those nations collapsed.
